newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China deity gets love, not money, from Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China deity gets love, not money, from Taiwan.

text.p: The revered statue of China's goddess Matsu finished a tour of Taiwan on Monday.
But while the statue received a divine reception during its tour, it was less successful in procuring more mundane offerings -- like money.
Thousands of worshippers lined the streets to greet a drum-beating cavalcade that sent the gold-plated figure off to the southern Kaohsiung airport, the last stop in its 100-day Taiwan sojourn.

The statue, considered by many to be the goddess herself, had arrived in Taiwan under similar pomp in January to begin a visit that easily became the largest recent cultural exchange between political rivals Taiwan and China.

But when the goddess and its delegation left on Monday, they found that Taiwan idolaters had donated only 95 gold plates and T$90,000 (US$3,200) to the goddess -- money to be used by the statue's home shrine in China's outlying Meizhou island.
"I thought it was impossible to collect so little money," said Chen Shih-yung, a Taiwan temple official responsible for arranging the statue's tour.

In Taiwanese and Chinese folk religions, it is common for worshippers to donate to religious leaders or figures. For example, when Tibet's exiled God-king the Dalai Lama visited in March, Taiwanese donated US$500,000 even though his tour was not billed as a fund-raiser.
And while the Matsu statue visit was not a fund-raiser either, the Taiwanese press has expressed shock that the figure raised so little.
One of the life-sized statue's mainland caretakers offered a diplomatic explanation, saying it was love, not lucre, that counted.
"I think the worshippers in Taiwan are very pious towards Matsu. Their love for Matsu cannot be measured by gold plates," Chen Jinpeng, assistant leader of China's delegation, said before departing.
Matsu has been worshipped by Chinese for centuries, her legend passed through the generations as folklore.
The most common version is that of a girl who became guardian to seafarers after she failed to save her father from drowning in choppy waters off China's southeastern coast.

Although Taiwan and China have been political rivals since they split after a civil war in 1949, the two sides have enjoyed strong cultural and economic ties following an unofficial thaw in the 1980s.
